audits.mathematicalReason: Of A's residents, 100 − 100/4 − 100/5 = 55 work in A. The incoming workers from B and C number 120/3 = 40 and 160/8 = 20. Therefore 55 + 40 + 20 = 115 people work in A. Fraction multiplication and the stated part–whole relationships directly support this calculation.

figureEvidence.fact: The arrows used are A→B labeled 1/4, A→C labeled 1/5, B→A labeled 1/3, and C→A labeled 1/8.

audits.mathematicalReason: The 120° hexagon angles make each removed corner triangle equilateral. The example therefore gives the enclosing triangle side length 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. Let the three corner-cut lengths be positive integers x, y, z. The remaining sides have lengths 6−x−y, 6−y−z, and 6−z−x, all positive. Triangle rotations and reflections permit the canonical ordering x≤y≤z, leaving y+z≤5. The possibilities are (1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,1,3), (1,1,4), (1,2,2), (1,2,3), (2,2,2), and (2,2,3): four with y=1 and 2·2 with y=2. Their hexagons have distinct side-length multisets, so there are no additional congruence identifications. This validates both the symmetry scope and the supporting geometry and integer enumeration.

figureEvidence.fact: The example has corner-cut edges of lengths 1 at A, 2 at B, and 2 at C. The hexagon edges lying along AB, BC, and CA have lengths 3, 2, and 3, respectively.

routes.label: Rule out smaller cube clusters directly
Use degrees in the face-contact graph

audits.mathematicalReason: An assembly of fewer than four cubes cannot work. In such a small assembly, both shaded faces of every cube would need face-contact neighbors, giving minimum contact degree at least two. Three cubes cannot form a face-contact triangle: neighbors covering two adjacent faces of one cube do not share a face with each other. Four cubes do work in a 2×2×1 slab, with each cube oriented so its two shaded faces are its two internal contact faces. This proves the lower bound and supplies an attaining construction. Both the direct-placement and contact-graph routes are defensible.

figureEvidence.fact: The illustrated shaded faces are adjacent. The lower drawing joins two cubes across an entire face, making one shaded face internal and leaving three shaded exterior faces.

audits.mathematicalReason: There are 6!/(3!2!) = 60 labeled paintings. Neither nonidentity rotation fixes a painting because there is exactly one green disk. Each reflection has two fixed disks and two exchanged pairs. A fixed painting puts green on either fixed disk, blue on the other, and assigns blue and red to the two exchanged pairs in either order: four paintings per reflection. The orbit count is therefore (60 + 3·4)/6 = 12. Alternatively, green has two position types, corner and side midpoint; each contributes (C(5,2)+2)/2 = 6 paintings. Both proposed routes account for reflection-symmetric paintings correctly.

figureEvidence.fact: The six disk centers occupy the three corners and three side midpoints of an equilateral triangle. Each reflection fixes a corner disk and the opposite midpoint disk while exchanging the other four disks in two pairs.

audits.mathematicalReason: Since BD = DC, triangle BCD is isosceles with base BC, so ∠DBC = ∠BCD = 70°. Because DA extends DC through D, ∠ADB is an exterior angle of triangle BCD and equals 70° + 70° = 140°. The selected isosceles-triangle and exterior-angle scopes exactly support this route.

figureEvidence.fact: A, D, and C lie on one straight baseline with D between A and C. Segment BD is drawn, and ∠BCD is labeled 70°. The equality BD = DC is supplied by the stem, not by diagram tick marks.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the center digit be j and the common opposite-pair sum be p. Since the digits total 45, 4p = 45−j, so j≡1 modulo 4 and j is 1, 5, or 9. The corresponding pair sums are 11, 10, and 9; in each case the remaining digits form four uniquely determined complementary pairs. Assign those pairs to the four labeled lines in 4! ways and orient each pair in 2 ways. Summing the three center cases gives 3·4!·2^4 = 1152. The vertices are labeled, and the problem does not identify rotated or reflected assignments, so no symmetry division is appropriate.

figureEvidence.fact: The vertices are labeled cyclically A through H around center J. The opposite vertex pairs are A/E, B/F, C/G, and D/H.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the square side be s, AD=h, AB=w, and the overlap area be I=sh. Recovering the whole areas from the percentages gives wh=2I and s²=5I. Since all lengths are positive, substitution and cancellation yield w=2s and h=s/5. Thus AB/AD=w/h=10. The rectangle/square area formulas, inverse-percentage calculation, and ratio interpretation are all used as mapped.

figureEvidence.fact: A and D lie on square side EH, and rectangle sides AB and DC cross FG. Consequently the intersection is a rectangular strip of height AD spanning the square's full width EF. No equality of the margins above and below the strip is needed.

audits.mathematicalReason: For radius r, the inscribed square has diagonal 2r and area 2r² by the Pythagorean theorem. Thus the full circle-minus-square region has area (π−2)r². Equality of the shaded areas gives π−2 = (π−2)R²/4, hence R²=4. The radius is positive, so R=2 units. The alternative scaling route is also defensible: homothety supplies the common linear factor between the complete circle-and-square configurations, while the listed circle and square area formulas supply the squared area factor. Homothety alone is not being treated as an area-scaling theorem, and neither optional method is universally required.

figureEvidence.fact: Each square has all four vertices on its circle. All four circle segments outside the left square are shaded, but only one of the four corresponding segments is shaded on the right. The center-to-corner radii are labeled 1 and R.
